one_liner: Header-only C++14 macro emulation of N4286 stackless coroutines; resume costs about 6 ns versus 82 ns for Boost.Coroutine2.
what_it_does: Gives pre-C++20 compilers N4286-style (co_await draft) stackless coroutines: generators, recursive generators, tasks, shared/lazy tasks and async sync primitives (event, mutex, work_group, when_all/when_any). A coroutine is an ordinary function whose body sits between CO2_BEG(return_type, (captures), locals...) and CO2_END, with CO2_AWAIT/CO2_YIELD/CO2_SUSPEND/CO2_RETURN macros in place of keywords. It is not a drop-in for Boost.Coroutine2: the interface follows the coroutine TS (promise_type, coroutine_traits, awaiters), and coroutine<> is move-only rather than a raw handle.
how_it_is_fast: The macros turn the body into a resumable state machine: a heap frame (std::allocator by default, custom allocator via the new clause) holds the declared locals, and each suspend point is a `case __COUNTER__:` label in a switch on a stored `_co2_next` index (Duff's-device / protothread style). Resuming is one virtual run() call plus a jump through the switch, with no stack switch and no register save/restore, which is why it lands near native MSVC co_await (6 ns versus 5 ns) and far below Boost.Coroutine2's Boost.Context stack switch.
when_to_use: Maintaining an existing codebase on a pre-C++20 compiler (C++14 with Boost) that already uses CO2 for generators or async tasks.
Generators and asynchronous continuations where every suspend point is in the coroutine body itself, not in nested calls.
Tiny per-coroutine memory: frames hold only the declared locals plus a small awaiter buffer, versus a full stack per Boost.Coroutine2 coroutine.
Bridging callback APIs (ASIO via the sister library act, PPL or TBB task_group) into await-style code on old toolchains.
when_not_to_use: New code: the README itself says all major compilers now support C++20 coroutines and recommends against CO2; use native co_await or the author's successor COZ (zero-allocation).
You need to suspend from inside nested ordinary function calls (stackful semantics): only Boost.Coroutine2/Boost.Context or fiber libraries do that.

Codebases that cannot tolerate heavy macro restrictions: locals crossing suspend points must be declared in CO2_BEG, no () initializers, auto needs CO2_AUTO, return/try/switch need macro replacements.
Projects that need a maintained dependency: repository archived 2024-10-09.

integration.dependencies: Boost (Boost.Config, Boost.Assert, Boost.Preprocessor in the core header; Boost.Thread/Optional for the adapted headers)
integration.min_toolchain: C++14; benchmark run on VS2015 Update 3 with boost 1.63.0; GCC/Clang supported (statement-expression extension enables CO2_AWAIT as an expression)
integration.thread_safety: not documented for coroutine objects; task scheduling across threads is shown with PPL/TBB examples, and co2::mutex/event are coroutine-level sync primitives

gotchas: Awaits are statements, not expressions: CO2_AWAIT(something{temporaries}) lets temporaries die before resumption, unlike real co_await.
Awaiters larger than (sizeof(pointer)+sizeof(int))*2 bytes fall back to dynamic allocation; enlarge with CO2_TEMP_SIZE and define CO2_WARN_DYN_ALLOC to catch it.
Exceptions thrown while initializing locals propagate directly to the caller and bypass set_exception, since initialization runs before initial_suspend.

Benchmark compares stackless against stackful (open issue #4 says the comparison does not make sense without that context); the benchmark source names the test bench_coroutines2 while the README table prints bench_coroutine2. stack_allocator had a deallocate bug (issue #5, closed 2018).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick CO2 over stackful switchers like libaco, libcopp, minicoro or Boost.Coroutine2 only when you want stackless, per-frame-allocated coroutines with TS-style await on a pre-C++20 compiler; if you are on C++20, Boost.Cobalt or plain co_await supersede it.
verified_claims_summary: The README's Google Benchmark run of test/benchmark.cpp times one resume of a coroutine that suspends forever with an empty action: Boost.Coroutine2 pull_type 82 ns, CO2 6 ns, native MSVC co_await 5 ns, built with VS2015 Update 3, boost 1.63.0, 64-bit release, on an unnamed 4 x 3200 MHz CPU. That is about 13.7x versus Boost.Coroutine2 (derived from page data), but it compares a stackless switch with a stackful context switch.
status_note: Archived 2024-10-09 and self-declared obsolete in favour of C++20 coroutines and COZ, but BSL-1.0 and header-only, so existing users can keep vendoring it.
